newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Watchdog slams Dutch state aid to ailing firms.
newsitem.headline: Watchdog slams Dutch state aid to ailing firms.

text.p: The Dutch state failed to apply various rules set by parliament for supporting ailing companies in recent years and in some cases did not report properly to the European Commission, the watchdog body on Dutch government spending Algemene Rekenkamer or Audit Office said on Wednesday.
"The relation between the aid and employment was unknown and coherent support plans, which included a detailed perspective of the State's role, were lacking," the watchdog said in a report.
It investigated five cases in the years 1987-1994 where the Dutch provided aid to aircraft maker Fokker, car manufacturer NedCar and truckmaker DAF.
The Audit Office said Fokker received support in 1987, 1993 and 1994 without the previously set conditions being applied.
"Therefore this company could keep steering its own course for a long time," the watchdog said about the aircraft maker which went bankrupt in 1996.

It added that a so-called "techno-lease construction" in 1994, where Dutch Rabobank bought Fokker's technological know-how in return for tax benefits, had cost the state an amount of money in the form of missed taxes which considerably exceeded the 412 million guilders that Fokker received.
"This form of support did not give the state any influence in Fokker and sight of the cost per saved job seems to have been lost," the report said.

It added the techno-lease package was not properly reported to the Dutch parliament and the Economics Ministry failed to report it to the European Commission at all because it did not consider the deal to be a support measure.
But despite of this the EC has started an investigation, which has not yet been concluded.
"The risks of reporting incorrectly were underestimated," the watchdog said.
It said another case where the ministry had not properly informed the European Committee was with support to truckmaker DAF in 1993.
"The ministry had already committed itself by contract before the support was reported," the Audit Office said.
It said state support to ailing companies should in future be provided strictly in line with the rules and should not be based on decisions taken for just one particular occasion.
It recommended a clear strategy scenario should be drawn up for these cases.
The Audit Office said the Dutch Economics and Finance ministers had said they did not agree with the watchdog's standards and judgements.
"They (the ministers) also said the correctness of a large number of our conclusions raised question marks," it added.
Later today Dutch Economics Minister Hans Wijers will comment on the findings of the watchdog body in a press conference in The Hague.
